title: Curriculum and dependency map: what depends on what?
summary: A directed acyclic graph of topics, drawn left to right by level, with arrows from prerequisite to dependent and a colour for done, current and upcoming. It tells you what has to be learned first and what is open to learn next.

media.alt: Directed acyclic graph of eight topics in four levels from algebra and calculus to neural models, with completed, current and upcoming topics in different colours.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What depends on what?
read_the_figure.axes: No axes. Horizontal position is the level (1 to 4); arrows run from prerequisite to dependent, left to right. Fill: teal completed, amber current, dashed grey upcoming. A legend sits at the top right.
look_at: Which topics have no prerequisites (the left column)?
Which topic has the most prerequisites, and is it completed?
What is the current topic, and what does it unlock?
Does every arrow run left to right (is the graph acyclic)?
read_the_figure.proves: It proves what depends on what, as claimed by the author, and shows progress. It does not prove that the dependencies are genuine or complete, nor how long a topic takes.
if_wrong: Arrows without direction: it is not clear what comes first.
Dependencies that run backwards or in a loop: a cycle makes order impossible.
Status by colour only with no legend: completed and upcoming look alike for some readers.

terms.meaning: Directed acyclic graph: arrows with direction and no way to come back to a node by following them.
A topic that must be understood before another one.
Length of the longest chain of prerequisites leading to a topic, counting itself.
The longest chain from a start to the end; it sets the minimum number of steps.
A list of nodes in which every prerequisite comes before its dependents.

remember: Arrows point from prerequisite to dependent.
Level = 1 + the maximum level of the prerequisites.
A topic can start only when all its incoming arrows come from completed boxes.
Check the legend: fill and dash encode status.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Boxes are topics; horizontal position encodes level; arrows encode the prerequisite relation. Colour and line style encode status (teal solid completed, amber bold current, grey dashed upcoming), so that the status survives greyscale. The bottom arrow repeats the reading direction and the level labels sit below.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A body of knowledge is a set of dependencies and not a list. A left-to-right DAG shows the order and the parallelism at once: topics in the same column can be learned in any order, and an arrow tells why a topic is waiting. Marking status on the same picture says where you are and what is unlocked.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Which topics have no prerequisites? Algebra and calculus (level 1, left). Q2: Which topic has the most prerequisites? Four topics have two direct prerequisites (ODEs, numerics, optimization and neural models), but neural models has the most in total, because all seven other topics lead to it. Q3: What is current and what does it unlock? Numerics (amber, level 3) is current; it unlocks neural models only after optimization (dashed, level 3) is done too, so optimization is the other open topic, and it has all its prerequisites (ODEs, probability) completed.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Direction: the arrowheads and the prerequisite to dependent note carry the entire meaning. A map with undirected links is a picture of relatedness, not a plan.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A map shows the author's idea of dependency; real dependencies are fuzzy and some links (an arrow from probability to ODEs, say) are missing or only partial. Equal-sized boxes hide that topics take different times. Colour for status invites reading the route as a ranking. Layout (position within a column) carries no meaning but may be read as such. Arrows that cross make long chains hard to trace, and omitted links look like independence.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A prerequisite table (topic, requires) is exact and diffable. A Gantt chart (F12.5) shows the time dimension. A matrix of topic against topic with marks shows density of dependencies. A syllabus with levels is simpler if the structure is a tree.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add an estimated time per box, mark the critical path, and shade topics that are unlocked but not yet started.

steps.title: Level of a node in the DAG
steps.note: Here algebra, calculus: 1; ODEs, probability, linear systems: 2; numerics, optimization: 3; neural models: 4.

steps.title: Paths and the critical path
steps.note: The number of distinct routes from a start to the end node; here 6 routes to neural models, the longest has 4 nodes.

worked.title: Levels and routes in the curriculum DAG
worked.problem: Edges: algebra to linear systems and ODEs; calculus to ODEs and probability; linear systems to numerics; ODEs to numerics and optimization; probability to optimization; numerics and optimization to neural models. Find the level of neural models and the number of routes to it.

solution.text: Routes: add up routes through the two parents (3 each).

worked.answer: Level 4 and 6 distinct routes from the two starting topics (3 from algebra, 3 from calculus): any of them can be followed.

analyze.q: Linear systems and ODEs are both level 2. Does it matter which you study first?
If an arrow from probability to numerics were added, what would change?

evaluate.q: Is the map a good basis for a study plan?
evaluate.hint: What does it not say about effort and time?

create: Mark the critical path and add time estimates.
Redraw as a table and compare what is easier to read in each form.

checks.q: What does an arrow from ODEs to numerics mean?
checks.answer: ODEs are a prerequisite of numerics.

checks.q: A node has parents at levels 2 and 3. Its level?
An arrow is added from neural models back to algebra. What breaks?
checks.answer: The graph is no longer acyclic: algebra would depend on something that depends on it, so no valid study order exists.
